♻ ☆ Quicksviewer: An LMM with Early Video Compression using Annealed Gumbel-Softmax
Ji Qi, Yuan Yao, Yushi Bai, Bin Xu, Juanzi Li, Zhiyuan Liu, Tat-Seng Chua
Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) uniformly perceive video frames, creating computational inefficiency for videos with inherently varying temporal redundancy. This paper present **Quicksviewer**, an LMM with new perceiving paradigm that partitions a nonuniform redundant video into varying cubes using Gumbel Softmax, followed by a unified resampling for each cube to achieve efficient video understanding. We further propose a Gumbel-noise annealing strategy that enables stable end-to-end LMM training with the discrete cubing network. This simple and intuitive approach dynamically compress video online based on the momentum of frame differences, significantly reducing spatiotemporal complexity (overall 45$\times$ compression rate), while enabling efficient training with large receptive field. We train the model from a language backbone through three progressive stages, each incorporating lengthy videos on average of 420s/1fps thanks to the perceiving efficiency. With only 0.8M total video samples, our model outperforms contemporary LMMs with the same backbone and comparable parameters amount. An experiment in A/B pretraining with same backbone and training data shows that, w/ cubing achieves lower training loss and higher benchmark accuracy (+2.1) than the fixed partitioning baseline, strictly validating the benefits. Moreover, the front-loaded compression in encoding substantially reduces latency in the computationally expensive prefill and decoding, making it suited to mainstream EPD disaggregated inference deployment. Code: https://quicksviewer.github.io.
♻ ☆ Do Egocentric Video-Language Models Capture Both Hand- and Object-Centric Cues?
Masatoshi Tateno, Alexandros Stergiou, Risa Shinoda, Yoichi Sato, Dima Damen
Recognizing hand-object interactions (HOIs) requires capturing both hand dynamics and object transformations, which provide complementary information for distinguishing visually similar manipulations. However, Video-Language Models (VLMs) trained solely on egocentric videos tend to over-rely on hand appearance, struggling to distinguish interactions with similar visual appearances but different dynamics (e.g., taking vs. kneading dough). To better utilize complementary hand- and object-centric cues, we propose a learning paradigm with (i) hand-object masked training to encode both hand- and object-centric cues and learn their relationships through cross-cue reconstruction, and (ii) an HOI-dynamics-aware decoder that grounds each cue through auxiliary location and semantic predictions. To assess how effectively models leverage hand- and object-centric cues for action recognition, we introduce Cue-Isolated HOI (CI-HOI), which independently evaluates recognition performance based on each cue. To enable this evaluation, we curate the DEHOI testbed using video inpainting to selectively remove either hands or manipulated objects, allowing us to evaluate action recognition with each cue isolated. DEHOI reveals that existing VLMs trained only on egocentric video rely more on hand-centric cues than VLMs trained on more non-egocentric video data. We show that our training paradigm mitigates this hand-centric bias, outperforming VLMs trained on the same egocentric data across DEHOI, standard action recognition, and object state recognition benchmarks.
♻ ☆ Coordinate-Free Corridor Reconstruction and Field-of-View Framing Attribution for 3D Bilateral Coronary Artery Trees in CT Angiography
Zeyu Jia, Tong Wu, Bo Yao, Xin Ming
Bilateral coronary tree extraction from cardiac computed tomography angiography (CCTA) must transfer from cropped benchmarks to uncropped scans without territory swaps or lattice staircases. Using 35 training scans, we fix a coordinate-free three-dimensional network (597,032 parameters) and a flush-admissible 8.0 mm corridor solver refined by a learned medial offset. We evaluate once on 50 ImageCAS scans against Lee94 thinning skeletons and zero-shot on 40 ASOCA scans (20 healthy, 20 diseased; 80 trees) against Vascular Modeling Toolkit (VMTK) Voronoi consensus centerlines. On uncropped pericardial ASOCA scans, our method leads all comparators on per-artery Chamfer distance (6.90 mm automatic despite 14.22 mm ostium error; 7.05 vs. 9.11 mm seeded, $p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.0047$). It also leads 1 mm centerline F1 (51.42% and 51.56%, +13.21 to +29.08 percentage points [pp], $p_{\text{Holm}} \le 9.0 \times 10^{-4}$) at $1.66 \pm 0.07$ s/scan on an NVIDIA L4 graphics processor. In cropped ImageCAS boxes, it leads F1 (76.98%) while trailing 18--22 mm bridgers on mean distance (3.37 vs. 2.72--3.20 mm; none significant after Holm). Pitch-matched 1.19 mm zero-clutter controls show coarse pitch degrades matched U-Nets whereas fixed-frontend distance reversal requires pericardial clutter. Flush collar gating rescues 30/32 seeded ASOCA stubs (-7.97 mm), and the learned medial offset raises node (+2.72 to +5.11 pp; bias-corrected and accelerated 95% confidence interval [+2.42, +3.01] on ImageCAS) and curve (+1.87 to +4.40 pp) F1. Short corridors curb pericardial chaining while learned offsets lift centerlines off the lattice.

♻ ☆ Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Kayli Battel, Todd J Rowell, Patricio Reyes Gomez, Laporsha Dees, Emily Sumner, Avinash Balachandran, Guy Rosman
Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

♻ ☆ Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
Run Luo, Kuan Zhang, Qi Deng, Yukun Chen, Zhihao Yang, Yufei Zhang, Renrong Hu, Yi Zhang, Guiyu Ma, Tianyu Fan, Longze Chen, Hao Sun, Jiaming Li, Jiaming Yang, Xiaohao Liu, Tao Tan, Minzheng Wang, Hangtian Jia, Shuai Yuan, Lvdi Wang, Xiao Liu, Chao Ma, Yuting Zou, Yinhe Zheng, Xiaobo Xia, Dawei Jiang, Shaoqing Ren
We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.
♻ ☆ Graph-augmented Segmentation for Enhanced In-Situ Geometry Reconstruction of Complex Shapes in Laser Powder Bed Fusion
Stefano Raimondo, Matteo Bugatti, Marco Grasso
In situ geometric inspection in Laser Powder Bed Fusion of Metals (PBF-LB/M) opens new possibilities for anticipated defect detection and more efficient qualification. It relies on image segmentation to reconstruct layer-wise geometries and identify manufacturing deviations as the part is being built. However, existing approaches face a critical yet largely overlooked challenge: photometric out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, namely the ability to maintain reconstruction accuracy when image appearance differs from the conditions represented during model training. This study represents the first exploration of a graph-augmented U-Net architecture for in situ geometric inspection in PBF-LB/M. The hybrid network integrates a Graph Neural Network (GNN) within the bottleneck to enhance reconstruction robustness under photometric distribution shifts. It is evaluated against conventional U-Net and active contour segmentation methods using two experimental case studies involving different lattice geometries, materials, and manufacturing setups, with X-ray computed tomography providing reference geometries. Generalization is assessed across different training and inference conditions and under controlled image perturbations. Results show that the UNet-GNN achieves higher reconstruction accuracy and consistency than the benchmark methods, with more pronounced improvements when training and inference conditions differ. Its advantages are confirmed across both case studies and under controlled photometric perturbations, while preliminary anomaly detection experiments indicate that improved robustness does not necessarily compromise sensitivity to geometric deviations. These findings highlight graph augmentation as a promising strategy for more reliable in situ geometric inspection under heterogeneous manufacturing conditions.

♻ ☆ OmniEdit-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Instruction-based Video Editing
Chenxuan Miao, Yutong Feng, Yi Lu, Yunfeng Yan, Donglian Qi, Shiwei Zhang, Yu Liu, Xi Chen, Hengshuang Zhao
Instruction-based video editing (IVE) offers diverse applications, yet evaluating editing models remains challenging. Existing benchmarks suffer from two key limitations: narrow task coverage inherited from image editing that overlooks video-specific dimensions, and metrics that inadequately capture instruction fidelity, allowing visually plausible but incorrect edits to receive high scores. To address these limitations, we introduce OmniEdit-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark covering spatial, temporal, audio, and reference-based editing. It distinguishes between explicit and implicit instructions and incorporates reasoning-based scenarios to reflect real-world editing requirements. We further propose an evaluation framework that assesses accuracy, preservation, realism, and consistency using both human judges and a state-of-the-art vision-language model (VLM). An accuracy-aware penalty mechanism conditions the other three scores on accuracy, prioritizing instruction fidelity and penalizing plausible but incorrect edits. Experiments on prominent open-source and commercial IVE models reveal substantial room for improvement. OmniEdit-Bench provides a structured testbed for identifying model limitations and advancing instruction-based video editing. Project page: https://omniedit-bench.github.io.
♻ ☆ VidDub: Replacement-Aware Supervision for Two-Step Video Dubbing
Yexin Liu, Yunlong Lin, Zehan Wang, Guangxin He, Xinli Xu, Jiajun Zha, Yaofu Liu, Yueze Wang, Bowen Ping, Yuanming Li, Amie Wang, Bernard Ghanem, Bing Li, Harry Yang
Video dubbing aims to synthesize lip movements that match target speech while preserving the speaker identity, head pose, and background of a source video. Existing editors are predominantly trained via self-reconstruction under original paired audio, even though the source mouth becomes a conflicting target when driving speech is replaced. We introduce \emph{replacement-aware cross-audio supervision}: paired-audio samples use full-frame reconstruction, whereas unpaired replacement-audio samples mask out source-mouth reconstruction losses and supervise the mouth solely through audio--visual synchronization while preserving unmasked facial regions and background. Because offline dubbing provides the complete source video and target speech beforehand, we present \method, a full-context diffusion editor that uses matched trajectory regression to transfer CFG-guided teacher trajectories to a two-step student and distribution matching to recover visual quality after compression. We will release the curated training dataset, VidDub-Bench, fixed paired- and cross-audio evaluation manifests, preprocessing outputs, and unified evaluation code. Across three training seeds, masking out conflicting source-mouth reconstruction improves cross-audio Sync-C by 0.833. At two NFE, the final student provides the strongest cross-audio synchronization and visual-speech recognition among the evaluated methods, with competitive visual fidelity and source preservation.

♻ ☆ Ischemic Stroke Segmentation and Net Water Uptake Quantification on Multicenter Non-Contrast CT Using Supervised Target-Domain Adaptation
Linus Britt, Maximilian Nielsen, Susan Klapproth, Andre Kemmling, Michael H. Lev, Gabriel Broocks, Rene Werner, Thilo Sentker
Quantitative assessment of infarct hypodensity on non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT), including net water uptake (NWU), requires manual or semi-manual lesion delineation, often guided by CT perfusion or diffusion-weighted MRI, limiting clinical applicability. Automated NCCT segmentation could enable such biomarker extraction but remains challenging across heterogeneous multicenter data. This study developed and externally tested a deep learning framework for ischemic stroke segmentation and NWU quantification on NCCT. In this retrospective multicenter study of 801 patients from four datasets, an nnU-Net-based model with foundation-model initialization, extended by modules comparing local features with the contralateral hemisphere, was trained on NCCT scans from the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf and the Acute Ischemic Stroke Dataset. The model was fine-tuned on target-domain subsets of the Boston (n=11) and ISLES (n=75) datasets, with evaluation on held-out cases. Segmentations and NWU were compared with expert references. Internally, mean Dice increased from 0.53 (conventional nnU-Net) to 0.57 (proposed approach). After fine-tuning, the proposed approach achieved median Dice of 0.56 for acute lesion segmentation (Boston) and 0.26 for post-treatment final-infarct prediction (ISLES), where small lesions predominated. For lesions >=30 mL, median Dice increased to 0.67 and 0.57, respectively. On the Boston dataset, automated and reference NWU agreed (concordance correlation coefficient 0.93, mean absolute error 1.24 percentage points). Contralateral feature comparison and target-domain adaptation supported NCCT-only infarct segmentation across heterogeneous external cohorts, although performance was lower for post-treatment final-infarct prediction. The approach enabled low-error NWU quantification from baseline NCCT without advanced imaging or manual annotation.
♻ ☆ Visual Token Coding for Video Multimodal Large Language Models
Chenxin Fang, Tao Chen, JunChao You, Jun Peng, Yiyi Zhou, Rongrong Ji
In this paper, we propose a new token compression paradigm for video Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), termed Visual Token Coding ($VTC$). Inspired by classical video coding principles, e.g., HEVC, VTC performs structured compression by predicting the I/P frames of a video and measuring their frame-wise residuals to estimate token redundancy. Based on this base paradigm, we further extend VTC with a set of dynamic budgeting designs towards more cost-effective token coding, termed $VTC_{dy}$. To validate VTC and $VTC_{dy}$, we apply them to three MLLMs and conduct experiments on a set of video understanding benchmarks. The experimental results show that as a base paradigm, VTC can achieve an average performance retention of 98.4% on Qwen3-VL under a 50% token compression ratio, and the enhanced $VTC_{dy}$ can further improve the retention to 100.3%, outperforming a set of compared methods. Moreover, as a plug-and-play design, VTC requires no additional tuning of MLLMs for token coding. Our code is given in the supplementary materials.

♻ ☆ Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing
Chia-Ming Lee, Yu-Jou Hsiao, Ming-Ching Chang, Xin Li, Yu-Lun Liu, Chih-Chung Hsu
Hyperspectral images (HSI) preserve material evidence lost in RGB, yet 3D material identification from multi-view HSI faces two obstacles. Spectral Gaussian splatting reconstructs spectra accurately but leaves unmixing to per-pixel post-processing, while multi-view hyperspectral capture is costly and real datasets lack pixel-level material labels and sub-pixel proportions. We propose Spectral World Renderer (SWR), a material-aware explicit representation that unifies 3D spectral reconstruction and unmixing: it fits a Gaussian scaffold from RGB and decodes ray-Gaussian intersections into abundances over a shared endmember dictionary. Additionally, appearance guidance prevents spectrally similar materials from merging when intensity absorbs their brightness differences. Moreover, SWR requires no material-label supervision during training. To address the data gap, we further construct the SWR Benchmark (SWR-Bench): a coding-agent pipeline generates eight indoor and outdoor worlds from measured reflectance, aligning HSI with both annotations. SWR achieves the highest mIoU in all eight worlds and the highest mean PSNR on each real dataset. On an 11-class urban world, it trains at least 3.67x faster than unmixing baselines; rendering averages 34.9 joint spectral and label views/s over four worlds on a single RTX 4090.

A. de Almeida, Paulo Guilherme Molin, Catherine Torres de Almeida, Angélica F. Resende, Vinicius Castro Souza, Marcelo Antonio Pinho Ferreira, Cássio Toledo, Eben North Broadbent, Angelica Almeyda Zambrano, Laura Simões, Juliano van Melis, Ricardo Ribeiro Rodrigues, Pedro H. S. Height was predicted by a deep learning network fusing Sentinel-2 reflectance, Sentinel-1 and ALOS PALSAR backscatter and ALOS elevation, trained on 7,179 and tested on 1,793 patches (58,800 km$^2$) from a statewide airborne LiDAR campaign over São Paulo state, Brazil. On held-out test patches, the mean absolute error is 2.26 m at 10 m and 1.90 m at 30 m, and the model was validated at two LiDAR sites outside São Paulo. ♻ ☆ RadMatch: Auditable Radiology Report Evaluation via Finding-Level Matching
Charles Corbière, Léo Machado, Baptiste Callard, Aubin Charley, Korentin Le Floch, Martin J. Willemink, Pierre Manceron, Corentin Dancette
As AI systems are increasingly used to draft radiology reports, reliably evaluating their clinical quality remains a critical challenge. We introduce RadMatch, a multi-stage LLM-based framework that turns report evaluation into a structured, auditable finding-level record. It extracts findings from a reference and a candidate report, matches them by clinical equivalence, grades each match over ten clinical attributes, and gives every match and unmatched finding a verdict and a clinical-significance tier. To validate metrics on CT, we build and release MetricEval-BodyCT, the first public metric-evaluation benchmark of chest and abdomen CT reports annotated by radiologists error by error. On it and three chest X-ray benchmarks, RadMatch with an open 31B judge on consumer GPUs agrees with radiologists more closely than previous published metrics, and even reaches inter-expert agreement on ReXVal and on the significant errors of MetricEval-BodyCT. Radiologists auditing its decisions on 60 studies confirm 98.5% of its matches and 93.6% of the errors it counts. When used to evaluate state-of-the-art radiology report generation models, RadMatch shows that most CT models, unlike several chest X-ray models, actually leave more significant errors than an image-blind normal template, as their added unsupported findings outnumber the reference findings they correctly report. We provide RadMatch's code, its dashboard, the MetricEval-BodyCT dataset and all per-report scores.
♻ ☆ Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers
Hansheng Chen, Shengqu Cai, Jan Ackermann, Rayhan Zirvi, Gordon Wetzstein, Xinchen Yan, Leonidas Guibas
Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.

♻ ☆ FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds
Ching-Heng Cheng, Chia-Ming Lee, Ming-Ching Chang, Xin Li, Chih-Chung Hsu
Single-image refocusing changes the focal plane and depth of field of a photograph after capture. Users compare focal choices on one photograph, so content stability across edits matters alongside quality and speed. Recent generative methods rerun large diffusion models for every edit, even when they first restore an all-in-focus image, so content can change inconsistently between edits. Yet only this restoration is highly ill-posed and benefits from a generative prior, whereas rendering blur is largely determined by depth and the focal plane. We therefore propose FlashReFocus, which runs diffusion once per photograph and renders each edit with a lightweight network. A one-step diffusion deblurrer with a decoder refiner recovers fine detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality. The renderer uses an explicit defocus map for control and defocus-bias attention to promote information exchange between tokens with similar blur magnitudes. Because every edit reuses the same reconstruction, in-focus content stays consistent across edits, and editing the map enables tilt-shift and two-plane effects. We further collect 3CReal, a benchmark of 89 pairs from three camera-lens systems, to evaluate generalization to unseen optics. For zero-shot bokeh rendering on EBB! Val176 and 3CReal, FlashReFocus leads the evaluated methods in fidelity and perceptual quality. At 1536x1536, a complete refocus takes 2.45 s and each subsequent edit 0.46 s on one RTX PRO 6000.

♻ ☆ Graphene: A Lightweight Transformer with Ising Mean-Field Refinement for Image Super-Resolution
Seungki Hong, Taekwang Jang
This paper proposes Graphene, a lightweight image super-resolution architecture with two complementary feature refinement mechanisms: Ising-model-inspired local feature refinement using an Ising Refinement Block (IRB) and stage-history-based feature refinement using a History Attention (HistAttn) module. The IRB reuses attention output features and pre-softmax attention logits to construct signed pairwise token couplings within each local window, applies unrolled mean-field updates, and refines features through a gated residual correction. These signed couplings allow alignment and opposition between latent spins to modulate local feature refinement. Driving world models forecast what a vehicle's sensors will record next. With this matching, an apparent loss of the thermal model to persistence in fog disappears. On all 58 validation sequences in six weather conditions, post-trained RGB and thermal forecasts beat compression-matched persistence. Joint training lowers the LiDAR error at 2s by 2.1m at a small cost in camera fidelity, and only the tri-sensor model's LiDAR forecasts beat persistence in mean error. As such, a self-evolving world model can be realized via a generative model conditioned by various constraints, whose future predictions are refined through feedback. We further discuss two examples, i.e., drones and manipulators, as early embodied testbeds where wind, sensing limits, actuation delay, contact dynamics and recovery constraints can be systematically perturbed and verified. The central claim is that the framework of autonomous video generation for self-evolving world models should not be judged by video fidelity alone, but by whether the generated frames improve valid action under counterfactual interventions and various embodiment constraints.

☆ Insight into Parametric First-Order Ambisonics Upscaling in Time and Frequency Domains
Oded Levi, Boaz Rafaely
First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) offers a practical representation for spatial audio, but its low-order reproduction introduces distinct perceptual limitations during binaural rendering. While recent methods synthesize Higher-Order Ambisonics (HOA) from FOA to overcome these constraints, the importance and potential of early reflections in the upscaling process have not yet been comprehensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap and understand the potential of incorporating early reflections in FOA upscaling, this work develops an experimental framework that selectively upscales these reflections. By utilizing an energy-based criterion, the proposed framework identifies and selectively renders the strongest early reflections with high-order resolution. The selection mechanism is evaluated across three domains: long-term temporal, short-time temporal, and the joint time-frequency (TF) domain. Validation through objective metrics, including the Scale-Invariant Signal-to-Distortion Ratio (SI-SDR), the clarity index ($C_{50}$), and Interaural Cross-Correlation (IACC), alongside listening tests, demonstrates that the TF-domain provides superior performance. By exploiting the sparsity of speech, the TF approach maintains robust performance in complex multi-talker scenarios, providing insights into the benefits of early reflections for the design of future parametric and data-driven FOA upscaling methods.

Andong Li, Kun Zhou, Xiaodong Li, Chengshi Zheng

Second, motivated by range-null decomposition theory of Mel filtering in the magnitude-spectral domain, we introduce a phase-aware neural vocoder that incorporates degraded-phase prior, together with a quality-guided dual-phase strategy to adaptively mitigate the effects of unreliable phase information. Third, we devise a simple yet effective one-step fidelity-perception alignment strategy that fine-tunes the flow model with complementary constraints from fidelity and perception domains. Extensive experiments are conducted on DNS-Challenge, EARS, GSR, and URGENT benchmarks, and both objective and subjective results demonstrate promising performance on various intrusive and non-intrusive evaluation metrics. Additionally, a clinical-variable baseline generalizes more consistently (ROC-AUC $0.65-0.71$), indicating acquisition-specific variability in acoustics is a stronger driver of poor generalizability. In codas, click composition improves prediction of whole-coda acoustic form beyond timing. Comparing acoustic structure across very different vocal corpora is difficult because the recordings use different native event units, contain different amounts of sequence, and were collected under different conditions. We use the high-dimensional representations of frozen, pretrained audio encoders to measure acoustic diversity and temporal organization. Matched sampling gives each corpus the same opportunities to observe new acoustic forms and relationships between events, without changing its native event definition. We compare sperm-whale codas, human speech phones, Bengalese-finch syllables, and common-marmoset calls using 1,952 events and 1,700 adjacent pairs per comparison. Whale shows the fastest accumulation of encoder-defined acoustic groups, while Finch has the strongest repeated-sequence recurrence against ordinary within-block shuffles. Their neighboring-event dependence is closely matched under a source-and-position control. A second preceding event changes held-out prediction more favorably for Whale than for the other corpora, although Whale's standalone improvement remains uncertain. Waveform measurements recover several differences, but duration and acquisition-sensitive properties also contribute. Together, the findings show how pretrained representations can measure distinct forms of vocal organization, while waveform and source controls define the scope of the comparison.

♻ ☆ Score-Informed Transformer for Refining MIDI Velocity in Automatic Piano Transcription
Zhanhong He, Roberto Togneri, Defeng, Huang
MIDI velocity is crucial for capturing expressive dynamics in human performances. In practical scenarios, a music score with inaccurate velocities may be available alongside the performance audio (e.g., music education and free online archives), enabling the task of score-informed MIDI velocity estimation. In this work, we propose a modular, lightweight score-informed Transformer correction module that refines the velocity estimates of Automatic Music Transcription (AMT) systems. Leveraging high-quality expressive datasets for rigorous evaluation, we focus on piano transcription, integrating our module into multiple existing systems. Trained exclusively on the MAESTRO dataset, our method consistently reduces velocity errors and improves cross-dataset generalization to SMD and MAPS datasets. Under this training protocol, integrating our score-informed module with HPT (named Score-HPT) establishes a new state-of-the-art, outperforming existing score-informed methods and piano transcription models while adding only 1 M parameters. Furthermore, our framework remains robust to temporal misalignments caused by imperfect audio-score synchronization, a common real-world challenge.

Audio and Speech Processing 9
☆ Insight into Parametric First-Order Ambisonics Upscaling in Time and Frequency Domains
Oded Levi, Boaz Rafaely
First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) offers a practical representation for spatial audio, but its low-order reproduction introduces distinct perceptual limitations during binaural rendering. While recent methods synthesize Higher-Order Ambisonics (HOA) from FOA to overcome these constraints, the importance and potential of early reflections in the upscaling process have not yet been comprehensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap and understand the potential of incorporating early reflections in FOA upscaling, this work develops an experimental framework that selectively upscales these reflections. By utilizing an energy-based criterion, the proposed framework identifies and selectively renders the strongest early reflections with high-order resolution. The selection mechanism is evaluated across three domains: long-term temporal, short-time temporal, and the joint time-frequency (TF) domain. Validation through objective metrics, including the Scale-Invariant Signal-to-Distortion Ratio (SI-SDR), the clarity index ($C_{50}$), and Interaural Cross-Correlation (IACC), alongside listening tests, demonstrates that the TF-domain provides superior performance. By exploiting the sparsity of speech, the TF approach maintains robust performance in complex multi-talker scenarios, providing insights into the benefits of early reflections for the design of future parametric and data-driven FOA upscaling methods.

☆ Beyond Co-Generation: Rethinking Jointness in Joint Audio-Video Generation
Jihoo Jung, Ji-Hoon Kim, Suyeon Lee, Gia Thinh Pham, Joon Son Chung
Our aim is to advance the understanding of genuine audio-visual coordination in joint text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation, with particular emphasis on semantic consistency. Evaluating audio-visual consistency in T2AV generation is nontrivial, as detailed text prompts obscure whether such consistency stems from genuine cross-modal coordination or merely from independent text following. To isolate the former, we introduce intrinsic jointness: the ability of audio and video to produce the same realization for details left underspecified by the prompt. Using semantically underspecified prompts (e.g., "musical instrument playing" rather than "electric guitar playing"), we investigate four recent models and reveal their limited intrinsic jointness. To address this limitation, we propose JointREPA, a simple representation alignment-based post-training method to facilitate cross-modal coordination. Since existing benchmarks use semantically detailed prompts, we introduce UNSAIDBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate intrinsic jointness under semantic underspecification. Experiments across two distinct models and three benchmarks, including UNSAIDBench, demonstrate that JointREPA consistently improves semantic consistency.

☆ Pluggable Subband-Decoupled Fusion and Unlabeled Capture Prototype Calibration: Bridging High-SNR Null-Subcarrier Regrowth and Low-SNR Coherent Preambles for Cross-Domain IoT RF Fingerprinting
Fengchong Yao, Jianbing Li, Qing Liu, Kefeng Song, Haitao Li, Song Wang, Kunpeng Wang
Zero-overhead physical-layer authentication at edge wireless access points (APs) is vital for securing resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) transceivers against credential cloning, yet cross-domain IEEE 802.11a/g radio frequency fingerprint identification (RFFI) faces an acute signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) crossover. Power-amplifier spectral regrowth on unpopulated null subcarriers resists indoor multipath at high SNR but decays quadratically below the thermal noise floor, whereas populated active in-band preambles survive low SNR yet degrade under severe multipath, causing static fusion to lose up to 44.7 percentage points (pp). To our knowledge, we propose the first RFFI framework that dynamically modulates active in-band waveforms and unpopulated null-subcarrier regrowth via a blind physical SNR gate: Pluggable Gated Subband-Decoupled Fusion with Unlabeled Capture-Aware Prototype Calibration (GSDF-CAPC). Avoiding the 20-35 dB subband gradient imbalance of joint training, GSDF pairs any frozen pretrained host backbone with a 46.3K null-subcarrier plug-in encoder (NS-Branch), fusing scale-standardized logits and gate-warped spherical embeddings under a source-calibrated lag-64 thermal-SNR gate with exact low-SNR fallback. Over unlabeled target AP captures, forward-only unbalanced optimal-transport calibration (UOT-CAPC) aligns shifted prototypes under packet-arrival skew and recovers parameter-free balanced Sinkhorn (U-CAPC) at equipartition. Across DataPort-WiFi, WiSig, and ORBIT MobRFFI, zero-retrain GSDF wins all 72/72 paired runs across eight backbones with 0.00 pp low-SNR loss, while edge IB-Host + GSDF (92.6K-93.3K active parameters, 1.82 ms single-core CPU latency) and timing-synchronized GSDF-STO / GSDF-Tri reach 57.50%-65.05% three-benchmark Macro-F1 (89.04%-100.00% over 5-10-packet IoT bursts).
☆ Personalized Causal Low-Bitrate Coded Speech Restoration with Speaker Embeddings
Eray Özgünay, Christian Rollwage, Kishan Gupta, Andreas Brendel, Xavier Domont, Mattes Ohlenbusch, Jan Rennies, Simon Doclo
Legacy low-bitrate speech codecs such as AMR-NB remain widely used in telephony, where they restrict speech bandwidth and degrade listening quality. Coded speech restoration (CSR) aims to restore the speech bandwidth while improving the overall quality of coded speech, but typically without adapting to different speakers. In this paper, we systematically investigate personalization for restoration of speech coded at low bitrates, using a causal, low-complexity Universal Bandwidth Extension Generative Adversarial Network (UBGAN) model as the basis. We propose two personalization methods based on speaker embeddings, which incur little additional computational cost at inference: (i) conditioning a single CSR model on speaker embeddings, and (ii) cluster-based model selection, where multiple personalized models are trained on clusters of acoustically similar speakers. Experiments are performed on AMR-NB coded speech at 4.75 kbps. Experimental results with disjoint seen- and unseen-speaker test sets show that cluster-based model selection does not consistently outperform the non-personalized UBGAN baseline, whereas embedding conditioning significantly improves ViSQOL and WB-PESQ scores for both seen and unseen speakers.

♻ ☆ Why ML-based cough models do not generalize: a systematic cross-dataset evaluation for tuberculosis screening
Wensi Zhang, Tomas Teijeiro, Jérôme Thevenot, David Atienza
Cough acoustics are promising for non-invasive tuberculosis (TB) screening, yet whether machine learning (ML) models capture disease-related acoustics or artifacts of data collection remains unresolved. We evaluated the cross-dataset generalizability of classical ML and deep learning (DL) cough-based TB classifiers across three independent datasets. Despite moderate within-dataset performance (ROC-AUC up to $0.76 \pm 0.06$), both pipelines fail to generalize, with external performance frequently below 0.6, indicating a possible limitation of the data. We further observed that audio representations are organized by recording device and dataset rather than TB status, predicted TB probability tracks country-level prevalence in CODA, and device mismatch degrades transfer while device-diverse training improves it. Additionally, a clinical-variable baseline generalizes more consistently (ROC-AUC $0.65-0.71$), indicating acquisition-specific variability in acoustics is a stronger driver of poor generalizability. High within-dataset performance is not enough. External validation is essential before cough-based TB models are clinically ready.
♻ ☆ A 1000-hour EEG-EMG-audio dataset of Japanese speech production
Motoshige Sato, Ilya Horiguchi, Masakazu Inoue, Kenichi Tomeoka, Eri Hatakeyama, Yuya Kita, Atsushi Yamamoto, Ippei Fujisawa, Shuntaro Sasai
We present a multimodal dataset of 1020 hours of simultaneously recorded scalp electroencephalography (EEG), facial electromyography (EMG), and speech audio from three healthy native Japanese speakers during open-vocabulary overt speech, covert repetition and speech listening. Recordings were acquired in many sessions over several months with three EEG systems of 61-128 channels, an ultra-high-density system (g.Pangolin) and two cap-type systems (g.SCARABEO and eego sports). Each session provides time-synchronized EEG, facial EMG, and audio, together with speech-event annotations and transcriptions. Although collected with speech decoding as a primary motivation, the dataset also supports work on multimodal signal processing, artifact modeling, longitudinal and cross-device adaptation, and EEG representation learning. Technical validation used power spectral density and event-related potential analyses to characterise spectral profiles and time-locked responses across participants, devices, and tasks. The dataset is available in Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) format from Harvard Dataverse under controlled access for research use. Its speech audio is voice-masked.

♻ ☆ AutoMV: An Automatic Multi-Agent System for Music Video Generation
Xiaoxuan Tang, Xinping Lei, Chaoran Zhu, Shiyun Chen, Ruibin Yuan, Yizhi Li, Changjae Oh, Ge Zhang, Wenhao Huang, Emmanouil Benetos, Yang Liu, Jiaheng Liu, Yinghao Ma
Turning a full song into a music video (MV) requires interpreting its lyrics, which are often metaphorical, multilingual, and repeated across choruses, together with its musical character, and laying the resulting imagery out along the song's structure. Existing music-to-video systems produce short clips or audio-reactive visuals and make little use of lyric meaning. We present AutoMV, a training-free multi-agent framework in which LLM Screenwriter and Director agents plan a full-song visual narrative from time-aligned lyrics and music analysis, keep characters consistent through a shared character bank, and route each shot to cinematic or lip-sync rendering with verification. To evaluate full-song MVs, we build M2VBench: 30 released songs paired with their official MVs, objective audio--visual metrics, and a 12-criterion rubric rated by music-industry experts. Expert evaluation shows that AutoMV outperforms other baselines, although a gap remains to human-produced MVs. Ablation studies highlight the importance of time-aligned lyrics for musical theme alignment and storytelling. We further find that the selected multimodal judge, guided by our evaluation rubric, recovers the expert ranking of automatic systems, with some discrepancies in fine-grained assessments.
♻ ☆ Who Says What: Symbolic Trimodal Binding Mechanisms in Audio-Visual LLMs NeurIPS 2026
Jihoo Jung, Youngjoon Jang, Joon Son Chung
Current Audio-Visual LLMs (AVLLMs) struggle with reasoning over videos featuring multi-speaker dialogues. In such videos, resolving "who says what" is crucial, which necessitates trimodal (text-audio-visual) binding. Motivated by these challenges, we systematically investigate how this trimodal binding is achieved in AVLLMs. Specifically, we identify emergent symbolic trimodal binding mechanisms in AVLLMs that utilize modality-specific symbolic variables. By encoding auditory and visual components into symbolic variables-capturing temporal utterance sequences and spatial entity coordinates, respectively-the model establishes cross-modal linking within this abstract space. Crucially, we reveal that when trimodal binding fails, the breakdown predominantly stems from misaligned audio-visual connections. To overcome this bottleneck, we introduce an audio-visual prompting method utilizing an off-the-shelf Active Speaker Detection (ASD) model. By simply overlaying visual bounding boxes on active speakers, this training-free approach yields immediate performance gains across four conversation-centric benchmarks. Moreover, lightweight fine-tuning of fewer than 300 steps on these ASD-prompted-videos extends these gains to three general AV benchmarks, suggesting the generalizability of our method. Our code is available at https://github.com/kaistmm/Who-Says-What.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition 150
☆ Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
Rui Ning, Om Chabra, Hari Balakrishnan
Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.
☆ FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency
Gene Chou, Guandao Yang, Fujun Luan, Lars Mescheder, Wei Dong, Stephan Richter, Vladlen Koltun
Autoregressive video diffusion models generate frames based on new observations and inputs, making them a promising medium for interactive visual experiences. However, existing models are orders of magnitude too slow for fluid interaction. This paper introduces FastFrames, a family of fast autoregressive video diffusion models that achieves interactive latency without compromising quality. We profile the inference pipeline of state-of-the-art models and find that operations often treated as fixed implementation details, such as VAE decoding and KV cache updates, in fact account for over half of end-to-end inference latency. We challenge the assumption that these components are indispensable and replace them with lightweight alternatives. Our 1.3B variant runs at 36 ms per frame, or 28 responses per second (RPS), on a single B200 GPU while matching the generation quality of a state-of-the-art model that is nearly 8x slower. Our 14B variant runs at 45 ms per frame, or 22 RPS, on an 8x B200 GPU node and yields significantly better visual quality and realism. We show that FastFrames enables real-time interaction in applications such as camera-conditioned and physics-conditioned video generation.

☆ EviSlide-MIL: Multi-Query Pooling and Shared Prediction for Class-Incremental Whole-Slide Image Classification
Zhouhan Qian, Sicheng Chen, Chad Wong, Tianyi Zhang, Enhui Chai, Zeyu Liu, Fei Xia
Histopathological analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs) plays a critical role in cancer diagnosis, and multiple instance learning (MIL) is widely adopted for WSI analysis under weak supervision. As new tumor subtypes are introduced, extending existing MIL models requires learning new classes while retaining knowledge of previously learned ones. This presents a class-incremental learning challenge, where models must acquire new classes with limited access to historical training data and recognize all learned classes without task identifiers at inference. A major obstacle is forgetting, as updates to feature aggregation and prediction modules can degrade performance on previously learned classes. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{EviSlide-MIL}, a class-incremental WSI framework that integrates multiple learnable queries per class with a shared prediction module. The queries aggregate frozen patch features into class-specific representations, while the shared prediction module limits parameter growth across incremental stages. By freezing queries associated with previously learned classes, EviSlide-MIL preserves their attention patterns for identical inputs, while experience replay and knowledge distillation further mitigate forgetting as shared parameters are updated. Experiments on eight tumor subtypes from The Cancer Genome Atlas demonstrate that EviSlide-MIL achieves improved performance and reduced forgetting compared with competing methods across most learning settings, demonstrating its potential for scalable and knowledge-preserving WSI classification. Code and pretrained models will be released.
☆ Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Kayli Battel, Todd J Rowell, Patricio Reyes Gomez, Laporsha Dees, Emily Sumner, Avinash Balachandran, Guy Rosman
Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. Code and data will be available upon acceptance.

☆ Learning Grounded Reasoning from Human Gaze
Gabriel Sarch, Declan Campbell, Nicholas Budny, Kia Ghods, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Jonathan D. Cohen, Brenden M. Lake, Taylor W. Webb
Human visual reasoning is driven by systematic exploration and extraction of task-relevant visual evidence. Human gaze provides a window into this process, making gaze a useful source of guidance for visually-grounded reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs). However, human gaze also includes noise and redundancies that may transfer poorly to VLMs. In this work, we investigate how human gaze data can be effectively leveraged to improve visual reasoning in VLMs, while maintaining alignment with human behavior. We collect 7,109 human gaze trials from a diverse and challenging set of visual reasoning tasks, and train grounded reasoning models with different forms of gaze guidance. Across evaluations in chart understanding, visual search, and counting, we find that using human gaze as a prior for grounded reasoning consistently outperforms supervision using the full gaze sequence. Based on these findings, we introduce GGR (Gaze-Guided Reasoner), which achieves greater human alignment and more reliable visual grounding while matching or outperforming leading grounded-reasoning baselines in accuracy. Reinforcement learning further improves task accuracy, gaze alignment, and grounding quality despite using no gaze supervision. Behavioral analyses show that gaze supervised models exhibit more visual exploration before arriving at an answer. Our results suggest that the value of human gaze lies in guiding spatial exploration and shaping reasoning behavior without requiring complete imitation of human behavior.
☆ Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models
Aviv Yossef, Or Patashnik, Or Zamir
We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image's content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access.

☆ Reading Scene States: Uncovering Safety Failures in Vision-Language Models
Tongxi Wu, Yuyang Cheng, Jiacheng Xian, Menglin Yang, Kai Chen, Jian Zhang, Yang Gao
Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide harmful assistance by interpreting visual events, even without an explicit request for the underlying harmful objective. We identify this \textbf{scene-state safety vulnerability} and introduce \textbf{SceneSafetyBench}, comprising 375 image--question pairs spanning Initial, Medium, and Ultimate scene states and five visual presentations. Across eight VLMs, scene-state inputs elicit harmful assistance with attack success rates (ASRs) of 45.6--72.3\%. Comparative analysis across three VLMs shows that scene-state inputs most closely resemble QR-related images in their layer-wise safety-related signal profiles, while exhibiting lower average late-layer readouts and distinct signal dynamics during generation. To turn this vulnerability into a systematic attack, we propose \textbf{S3TA}, which translates harmful objectives into scene states, queries image--question pairs independently, and assembles the responses. On seven MM-SafetyBench categories across eight open-weight and commercial VLMs, S3TA achieves a model-average ASR of \textbf{71.2\%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.1 percentage points}. Text-side filters and visual moderation provide limited protection. These findings highlight the need to safeguard the assistance models infer through scene-grounded reasoning, beyond screening input content.

☆ Retrieval-Augmented Correction for Generalist Medical Image Segmentation
Vincenzo Marcianò, Xiaoming Zhang, Michela Antonelli, Sebastien Ourselin, Maria A Zuluaga
Automated segmentation is routinely used as the first step in quantitative image-based clinical workflows, where predicted masks are subsequently reviewed and corrected by human operators. Automated correction of the residual structural errors is currently addressed one anatomy at a time, so the number of trained correctors scales with the number of segmentation targets. We present GRACE, a retrieval-augmented refiner that edits an input mask under context drawn from a shared knowledge base of verified prior cases. The refiner is trained once on a multi-organ corpus spanning compact organs, cavities, branching vessels, and tumour lesions. In the held-out dataset-transfer evaluation, three held-out datasets query a fixed knowledge base built from training data only. A separate leave-one-anatomy-out experiment tests parameter-free index extension: verified cases of an unseen solid organ enter the knowledge base, and the refiner stays frozen. A light shape-aware projection head on a frozen multimodal encoder maps embedding similarity to the shape agreement of the masks, so the knowledge base returns cases that the refiner can use as a shape prior. We evaluate GRACE on 18 public datasets spanning CT, MRI and ultrasound, using nine refinement configurations and seven upstream segmentors that span weak, mid, and strong operating regimes. We report each change with the DSC of its input mask. On the weak tier, the input DSC is 0.386 and GRACE adds up to +0.35 DSC. On a strong segmentor, the input DSC is 0.932 and the mean change is small. Transfer to an imaging modality that is absent from training and from the index is partial and depends on the anatomy, and remains an open research direction. Our results suggest retrieval-conditioned refinement is a practical alternative to anatomy-specific correction models. Code: https://github.com/robustml-eurecom/grace

☆ Any2Building: Unifying Point Clouds and Images for Building Reconstruction via Shared Spatial Queries
Hongye Hou, Zhuoxiao Li, Liu Xiangyu, Tengxi Wang, Jing Ou, Dongli Wu, Shuai Zhang, Tongyan Hua, Wufan Zhao
Abstracting structured buildings from limited observations is essential for 3D urban modeling and digital twins. Partial point clouds and overhead images of the same building provide incomplete 3D surface measurements and visual cues to its footprint, roof geometry, and rooftop structures, respectively. This motivates a unified framework that aligns geometric and visual cues in 3D and reconstructs buildings from either or both modalities. Building on this connection, we present Any2Building, a unified model for Level of Detail 2 (LoD2) building reconstruction from partial point clouds, overhead images, or both, with optional coarse geometric priors. At its core is an occupancy-grounded shared spatial queries representation that organizes available observations within a common 3D grid. Supervised by complete building surface voxels, these queries connect observational evidence to target geometry, enabling a shared generator to learn structural priors across tasks and providing spatial guidance for recovering missing structure. A trained voxel conditional surface-generation and low-poly remeshing pipeline then converts the predicted structure into compact LoD2 building models. To support this framework, we introduce BuildingWorld-Image, comprising approximately one million paired samples of partial point clouds, overhead images, and LoD2 building models across 18 cities. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that Any2Building outperforms existing methods in geometric reconstruction accuracy across unimodal and multimodal point-cloud completion, single-image building generation, and prior-assisted generation, while maintaining detailed and robust recovery when point cloud input modality is degraded.
☆ Say Less, Hallucinate Less? Diagnosing and Restoring Object Coverage in Preference-Optimized Vision-Language Models
Hansang Lee
Preference optimization (PO) is the standard way to reduce object hallucination in large vision-language models. We find that four public PO checkpoints of LLaVA-1.5-7B also lower object coverage. They name fewer object categories, and their lower hallucination rates bring no significant gain in set-level object F1 on CHAIR. We therefore ask how much of the PO gain the base model can reproduce by stopping earlier. A positive end-of-sequence (EOS) logit bias lets the base model reach the recall of each PO model, and this early stopping alone reproduces 58 to 86 percent of the CHAIRi gain of three checkpoints on two disjoint COCO sets. Writing longer does not bring the lost categories back. Under greedy decoding, a negative EOS bias recovers only 2 to 9 percent of the lost CHAIR recall of these checkpoints, and 94 to 96 percent of the added object mentions repeat categories already named. On CHAIR, the base caption of the same image still names about half of the missed object categories. We therefore propose base-guided object-category restoration, which appends high-confidence base-only categories to the PO caption without training. With thresholds fixed on a development set, it brings three checkpoints within one point of the base recall on a held-out COCO set with a lower distinct-object hallucination rate than the base model. Against the recall-matched base stopping curve, its gain holds for RLAIF-V near the base recall and for RLAIF-V and CHAIR-DPO at an intermediate recall. We will release the code of the recall-controlled evaluation.

☆ Déjà View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks
Mranmay Shetty, Gabriel Kreiman
A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.

☆ Attribution Through the Decoder: Prediction-Space Explanations for Structured Outputs
Zaer Bin Zaqy, Brinnae Bent
Networks that predict angles, gaze directions, and rotations do not output these quantities directly: they emit raw coordinates that a fixed decoder, such as normalization, maps to the final prediction. Attribution methods are usually applied to the raw coordinates, so they can credit inputs for changes the decoder discards, such as rescaling a vector when only its direction matters. The resulting explanation can highlight inputs that have no effect on the prediction. We instead attribute through the decoder differential, which for normalization decoders reduces to a scaled tangent projection. We characterize invariance to output rescaling, show that every fixed smooth scalar target on a sphere has points of zero tangential sensitivity, and show that an endpoint-projected variant of Integrated Gradients can still attribute to scale-only inputs, whereas direct angular Integrated Gradients cannot. On synthetic tasks with analytically known relevance, ambient attribution assigns up to 72% of its mass to an irrelevant region. On MPIIGaze validation data, tangent Grad-CAM produces 44% greater prediction displacement under 10% pixel deletion. On PASCAL3D+ with a 6D rotation decoder, the full differential improves mean deletion displacement by 14.1 degrees over the ambient coordinate sum and by 13.8 degrees over a decoder-invariant scalar. Results for a two-polarity tangent LayerCAM variant are mixed: it exceeds ambient-sum LayerCAM on circular regression but no difference is detected on quaternion pose. These results separate two failure sources, radial contamination and scalarization loss. The approach uses existing attribution methods with decoder-aware targets, although some variants also require changes to attribution aggregation. An invariant attribution can still miss inputs that drive the prediction, so invariance and deletion performance should each be checked.
comment: Under review
☆ TextSphere: Efficient Text-to-Image Generation via Shared Hyperspherical Alignment and Uniformity
Yixia Zhang, Girish A. Koushik, Xilu Wang, Wenwu Wang
Recent advances in text-to-image generation have substantially improved image quality, particularly through diffusion-based methods that require multiple inference steps. In contrast, Sphere Encoder offers an efficient generative framework capable of producing images with fewer forward steps. However, extending it to free-form text is nontrivial, because its class-conditioned design lacks cross-modal alignment. To address this challenge, we propose TextSphere, an efficient text-to-image generative framework that extends Sphere Encoder with language conditioning and cross-modal alignment. We incorporate pretrained CLIP text embeddings through adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) to guide image generation while retaining the original spherical sampling mechanism. To bridge the cross-modal representation gap, we introduce a Spherical Semantic Alignment and Uniformity (SSAU) objective that jointly promotes semantic alignment and representation uniformity on the hypersphere. Experiments on CUB-200-2011, MS-COCO-2014, and Flickr30k demonstrate that TextSphere consistently reduces generation FID (gFID) over the text-conditioned baseline while achieving reconstruction FID (rFID) below 1.0. With only 4 and 6 sampling steps, TextSphere achieves lower gFID than the compared diffusion- and GAN-based models trained from scratch on CUB-200-2011 and MS-COCO-2014, respectively. We further observe that improved reconstruction fidelity does not necessarily yield better generation quality. In addition, we use Partial Least Squares Singular Value Decomposition (PLS-SVD) to analyze cross-modal alignment and modality gap, offering insight into the effectiveness of our approach.

☆ VIVID: Beyond Static Multi-Image Reasoning with Localized Visual Differences and Textual Entity Dynamics in Video MLLMs
Chengqian Ma, Yuanze Zeng, Hongyu Wang, Mingfeng Lin, YiCheng Xiao, Yu Chen, Pengyu Li, WenHao Wang, Yuexiao Ma, Xiawu Zheng, Fei Chao
Video question answering under tight frame budgets requires preserving localized motion and event order, yet current video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reduce comprehension to static multi-image reasoning by discarding unselected frames and encoding keyframes independently: (1) Spatially, whole-frame pooling dilutes small moving targets into static backgrounds; (2) Temporally, dropping intermediate frames or averaging tokens erases inter-frame motion, confusing direction, speed, and order. We propose VIVID (Visual Inter-frame Variations and Individual Dynamics), which moves beyond static snapshots like human vision: keyframes capture core states while inter-frame Patch Diffs preserve neighboring changes within $K_f$ keyframes. Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning (ADKP) selects anchors from a $3\text{ fps}$ pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory (DRCM), forming Dynamic Tokens at zero extra anchor tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion Region of Interest (ROI) and chronological Entity State Chains. Adding $0.22\%$ trainable parameters to a frozen $27\text{B}$ backbone, VIVID-Small ($50$ examples, $\sim 1.5$ GPU hours) beats all eleven baselines in overall accuracy across $8,083$ questions and trails only VIVID-Large ($3,600$ examples), which leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Code: https://github.com/step-out/VIVID
☆ $π^4$: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion
Yifan Wang, Weiguang Zhao, Ni Yang, Haoyu Guo, Junting Dong, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
$π^4$ is a unified foundation model for 4D scene perception. From diverse, uncalibrated RGB observations in the wild---a single image, an unordered collection, or a video sequence---it recovers dense geometry, camera poses, and metric scale, together with 2D/3D point tracks and moving-object masks for multi-image inputs. It couples a geometry branch with a geometry-conditioned motion branch, which predicts image-space correspondences that are lifted into 3D using reconstructed target-view geometry. Across diverse benchmarks, $π^4$ achieves the best overall average rank in geometry evaluation, alongside competitive performance in single- and multiview 2D/3D point tracking and moving-object segmentation. With a shared backbone, the full geometry-and-motion system contains approximately 0.5B parameters---less than half the size of most baselines. It produces joint reconstructions and tracks in one forward pass, including large-scale scenes with thousands of input images despite training with contexts of at most 64 views. We further present the data and training recipe underlying these capabilities, together with empirical studies of key design choices. Code and models are available at https://github.com/yyfz/Pi4.
☆ TCP4D: A Unified Tool-Center-Point Tracking and Generation Model for Robot Manipulation
Haosong Peng, Xiangyang Liu, Zhengshen Zhang, Yunfeng Fan, Tianyu Qi, Xin Xia, Yufeng Zhan, Wenchao Xu
Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.

☆ GameRealm: Grounding Visual Learning in Interactive Games
Weiguang Zhao, Yifan Wang, Ni Yang, Yating Wang, Xingyu Miao, Yankai Jiang, Mulin Yu, Tao Lu, Haoyu Guo, Junting Dong, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.
☆ The Illusion of Grounding: Do Vision-Language Models Weigh Retrieved Text and Images Like an Ideal Observer?
Basavaraj R M, Harshal Chandel
Retrieval-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) answer from two sources of evidence that can each fail: the retrieved text can be wrong or noisy, and the image can be degraded or contradicted. We introduce GIB-200K, 200,000 image-question items built from COCO and Visual Genome, each expanded into controlled stress conditions: hard-negative retrieval noise (1-20 documents), visual ambiguity (Gaussian and motion blur, low-resource crops) and cross-modal conflict with counterfactual flip pairs. Instead of only measuring degradation, we ask how models combine the two modalities. From ideal Bayesian cue combination we derive a testable prediction that yields formal definitions of Knowledge Inertia (text over-weighted relative to the model's own image evidence) and Sensory Capture (the reverse), and we estimate the weights with a measurement-error-corrected regression whose recovery of known weights we verify. A counterfactual flip decomposition separates modality bias from concept priors, and a Grounding Illusion Score measures how much clean accuracy is not grounded in the image. We evaluate 4 open models on one frozen, seeded evaluation split of 2,000 GIB-200K items. All models are accurate on clean inputs (92.5%-94.2%) but adverse accuracy falls to 41.3%-59.9%. The two LLaVA models over-weight the text (Knowledge Inertia, w_T/w_I = 1.229 and 1.322), whereas InternVL3 favours the image (w_T/w_I = 0.680); between 34.8% and 71.4% of the clean answers that are correct are abandoned when the document lies. A training-free consistency check that compares the answer with and without retrieval trades coverage for accuracy under misleading documents, while falling back to the image fails when the image is heavily degraded. All per-instance outputs, code, and an audit that recomputes every reported open-model number are released.

☆ Nunchi: Ears Help Eyes in Multi-Party Conversations
JunYeong Park, Shijing Wang, Seonwook Park, Michael Stengel, Shalini De Mello, Sang-Il Choi, Hyung Jin Chang
Identifying whom a person looks at is central to understanding multi-party conversations, yet gaze geometry alone becomes ambiguous as more people appear. Conversations offer cues that geometry lacks, such as who is speaking and what is said, but no gaze dataset provides them for many multi-party scenes. We introduce SORBET, a benchmark of 3,340 samples from 1,578 clips with synchronized speech, transcripts, and attended person labels, covering more multi-party scenes than existing gaze datasets. Prior gaze models struggle to use these cues, which come in different forms, must be linked to the right person, and can conflict with gaze geometry. We propose Nunchi, a framework that constructs a text prompt from the transcript and the outputs of gaze and speaker models, links every cue to the candidates with shared labels, and lets a vision-language model (VLM) weigh gaze geometry against conversational cues to identify the attended person. Nunchi outperforms the strongest existing method by 4.8 percentage points. On SORBET, conversational cues help whereas additional visual cues do not, and the gains hold across three VLMs, with automatic transcripts, and on two existing datasets.
